title: Finite Fourier Analysis and the Fast Fourier Transform

items.title: Orthogonality of the characters $x\mapsto e^{2\pi ikx/N}$ on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$
items.statement: Let $N\ge1$ and let $k,\ell\in\mathbb Z$. Then $$\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}=\begin{cases}N,&k\equiv\ell\pmod N,\\ 0,&k\not\equiv\ell\pmod N.\end{cases}$$ At $N=1$ the congruence holds for all $k,\ell$ and the sum is $1$. The sum is a finite sum of complex numbers ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]), and $N$ on the right is the image of the natural number $N$ in $\mathbb C$.

items.strategy:
Case split on the ratio $\omega:=e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)/N}$. If $k\equiv\ell\pmod N$ then $(k-\ell)x/N\in\mathbb Z$ for every integer $x$, so every summand $\omega^x$ equals $1$ by [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]; the sum of $N$ copies of $1$ in the additive monoid of $\mathbb C$ is $N\cdot1_{\mathbb C}=\iota(N)$ by the recursive definition of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] and [[lem-integer-multiples-agree-with-canonical-natural]]. If $k
ot\equiv\ell\pmod N$ then $(k-\ell)/N
otin\mathbb Z$, so $\omega
e1$, while $\omega^N=e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)}=1$ by the addition law and the kernel theorem; prove the complex geometric identity $1-\omega^n=(1-\omega)\sum_{x<n}\omega^x$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$ by induction on $n$ directly from the same recursion ([[thm-induction-principle]], [[lem-power-laws]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]), then insert $n=N$ and use $\omega^N=1$ and $1-\omega

This is the coincident-root/geometric-sum case split of Taylor §11; the real-variable factorisation lemma and the published representation-theoretic orthogonality are independent cross-checks, not dependencies, because both are stated outside the complex-sum setting used here. Include the $N=1$ clause explicitly, since the transform page must be total at length one.

items.title: The unitary discrete Fourier transform on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$
items.statement: Let $N\ge1$ and let $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ be the complex vector space of functions $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-function-space]], [[def-vector-space]]). For $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ define the **unitary discrete Fourier transform** $\mathcal F_Nf:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ by $$(\mathcal F_Nf)(k):=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,e^{-2\pi ikx/N},$$ where $[x]_N$ is the class of the integer $x$ and $N^{-1/2}$ is the rational power of [[def-rational-power]]. Then $(\mathcal F_Nf)(k+N)=(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$, so $\mathcal F_Nf$ is a well-defined function on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and $\mathcal F_N$ is a map $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}\to\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Equivalently $(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z/N}f(x)\,\chi_{-k}(x)$ with the characters $\chi_k([m])=\exp(2\pi ikm/N)$ of [[ex-pontryagin-dual-of-a-finite-cyclic-group]]. This fixes the negative-sign, $N^{-1/2}$-normalised convention of the page; the unnormalised engineering convention is [[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]].

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Fourier Analysis, Distributions, and Constant-Coefficient Linear PDE (author PDF)
references.locator: §11, PDF pp. 86-88: the transforms (11.1)-(11.2) and the unitary $L^2$ conventions (11.4)-(11.5), transposed from the multiplicative group $\Gamma_n$ to $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ with the sign and normalisation fixed as stated

references.title: MIT 18.310 lecture 23, The Finite Fourier Transform and the Fast Fourier Transform Algorithm (course page)
references.locator: heading 3: the finite Fourier transform as evaluation of a polynomial at the $n$-th roots of unity, and the symmetric forward/inverse forms

items.strategy: Well-definedness: the display sums over the $N$ representatives $0,\dots,N-1$, and [[ex-pontryagin-dual-of-a-finite-cyclic-group]] identifies $e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ with $\chi_{-k}([x]_N)$, so each summand depends only on $[x]_N$; reindexing by another representative list is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]]. Periodicity in $k$: $e^{-2\pi i(k+N)x/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ix}$ and $e^{-2\pi ix}=1$ for every integer $x$ because $-2\pi x\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]], [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]), so all summands are unchanged. The scalar $N^{-1/2}$ is legitimate because $N>0$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). State the linearity of $\mathcal F_N$ as part of the definitional content if needed; unitarity is proved separately in [[thm-finite-parseval-and-plancherel]] and is not assumed here.

items.title: The counting inner product on $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z}$
items.statement: Let $N\ge1$ and $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Define $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z/N}f(x)\,\overline{g(x)}=\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,\overline{g([x]_N)}.$$ This is the inner product on $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ induced by the counting measure on the finite group $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$: it is $\mathbb C$-linear in the first argument, conjugate-symmetric, and satisfies $\langle f,f\rangle=\sum_x|f(x)|^2\ge0$, with $\langle f,f\rangle=0$ if and only if $f=0$.

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Fourier Analysis, Distributions, and Constant-Coefficient Linear PDE (author PDF)
references.locator: §11, formula (11.5) and the following lines: $L^2$ pairings by counting measure on $\mathbb Z_n$ and $(1/n)$-weighted counting measure on $\Gamma_n$

references.title: Manfred Einsiedler and Thomas Ward, Ergodic Theory with a View Towards Number Theory, Appendix C (course-hosted full text)
references.locator: Appendix C.2-C.3, printed pp. 431-435: Haar measure on a discrete group is counting measure, and $\langle f_1,f_2\rangle=\int_Gf_1\overline{f_2}\,dm_G$

items.strategy: The two displays agree by reindexing the finite sum ([[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]]). Linearity in the first argument, conjugate symmetry and $\langle f,f\rangle=\sum_x|f(x)|^2$ follow from the recursive sum definition ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]) with the field laws ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) and the conjugation and modulus laws ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]); the axioms compared against are those of [[def-inner-product-space]] with the linear-first convention. Definiteness: enumerate $\mathbb Z/N$ as $[0],\dots,[N-1]$; each $|f([k])|^2$ is a nonnegative real and the sequential real sum $\sum_{k<N}|f([k])|^2$ vanishes only if every term vanishes ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], claim 4), while the group sum agrees with that sequential sum by the enumeration independence of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] and the reindexing rule of [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]]; hence $\langle f,f\rangle=0$ forces $|f(x)|=0$ and therefore $f(x)=0$ for every $x$. Counting measure enters only through the normalisation-free weight $\sum_x\delta_x$ on the finite discrete group ([[def-counting-measure]], [[ex-counting-measure-as-haar-measure-on-a-discrete-group]]); no factor $1/N$ is inserted, exactly as in Taylor (11.5) on the dual side.

items.title: The unnormalised cyclic convolution on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$
items.statement: Let $N\ge1$ and $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. The **cyclic convolution** of $f$ and $g$ (unnormalised: no factor $1/N$ or $1/\sqrt N$ is inserted) is the function $f*g:\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ defined by $$(f*g)(x):=\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z/N}f(y)\,g(x-y),\qquad x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z,$$ where $x-y$ is the group operation of $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-integers-modulo-n-basic-algebra]]) and the sum is the finite sum over the group. The operation is commutative, and it is the convolution attached to the counting measure on the finite group.

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Fourier Analysis, Distributions, and Constant-Coefficient Linear PDE (author PDF)
references.locator: §11, formula (11.30) and its surroundings: discrete convolution and Fourier multipliers on $\Gamma_n$; the same construction is stated here on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$

references.title: MIT 18.310 lecture 23, The Finite Fourier Transform and the Fast Fourier Transform Algorithm (course page)
references.locator: headings 3-4: polynomial products and the Convolution viewpoint behind the transform

items.strategy: The value is a finite sum of complex numbers indexed by the finite group, hence well defined; $f(y)$ and $g(x-y)$ are values of functions on classes, so no representative is chosen. Commutativity: the substitution $z=x-y$ reindexes the finite sum by the bijection $y\mapsto x-y$ of $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]], [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]]) and gives $\sum_zg(z)f(x-z)$. No normalisation factor is included; the factor $\sqrt N$ in [[lem-finite-fourier-transform-converts-cyclic-convolution-to-scaled-product]] is the exact price of this convention. Distinguish this cyclic operation from linear convolution of finite sequences, which coincides with it only after sufficient zero padding ([[cex-linear-and-cyclic-convolution-are-not-the-same-without-zero-padding]]).

items.title: Finite Fourier inversion for the unitary transform on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$
items.statement: Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ $$f(x)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},$$ the right-hand side being independent of the chosen representative of $x$. Consequently $\mathcal F_N$ is bijective with inverse the positive-sign unitary transform $(\mathcal G_Ng)(x):=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}g(k)e^{2\pi ikx/N}$, and there is no convergence, regularity or support hypothesis.

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Fourier Analysis, Distributions, and Constant-Coefficient Linear PDE (author PDF)
references.locator: §11, Proposition 11.1 and formula (11.4): the inversion formula for $\Phi_n$, with inverse (11.2)

references.title: MIT 18.310 lecture 23, The Finite Fourier Transform and the Fast Fourier Transform Algorithm (course page)
references.locator: heading 3: the inverse transformation by multiplying each $p_k$ by $z^{-sk}$ and summing, giving $a_s=(1/n)\sum_kp_kz^{-sk}$

items.strategy: Substitute the definition of $\mathcal F_N$, interchange the two finite sums by the finite Fubini rule (part 3 of [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]]), moving the scalar factors through the inner sums by distributivity ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]), and evaluate the inner sum $\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}e^{-2\pi ik(y-x)/N}$ by [[lem-orthogonality-of-characters-on-a-finite-cyclic-group]]: it is $N$ when $y=x$ and $0$ otherwise. The outer sum over $y$ then collapses to $N^{-1/2}\cdot N^{-1/2}\cdot Nf(x)=f(x)$ using $N^{-1/2}N^{-1/2}=N^{-1}$ and $N\cdot N^{-1}=1$ ([[lem-rational-power-laws]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). The same computation with the roles of the two exponentials exchanged proves $\mathcal G_N\circ\mathcal F_N=\mathrm{id}$ and $\mathcal F_N\circ\mathcal G_N=\mathrm{id}$, so $\mathcal F_N$ is bijective; one of the two identities already suffices on the finite set $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Record that the right side is $N$-periodic in $x$ ([[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]).

items.title: Finite Parseval and Plancherel identity for the unitary DFT
items.statement: Let $N\ge1$ and $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then $$\langle\mathcal F_Nf,\mathcal F_Ng\rangle=\langle f,g\rangle,$$ where both pairings are the counting inner products of [[def-counting-inner-product-on-complex-functions-on-z-mod-n]]. In particular $\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}|(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)|^2=\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}|f(x)|^2$, so $\mathcal F_N$ preserves the counting inner product of [[def-counting-inner-product-on-complex-functions-on-z-mod-n]].

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Fourier Analysis, Distributions, and Constant-Coefficient Linear PDE (author PDF)
references.locator: §11, Proposition 11.1: $\Phi_n$ is a unitary isomorphism; formula (11.5) fixes the two inner products

references.title: Manfred Einsiedler and Thomas Ward, Ergodic Theory with a View Towards Number Theory, Appendix C (course-hosted full text)
references.locator: Appendix C.3, printed p. 435: the Parseval formula $\langle f,g\rangle_G=\langle\widehat f,\widehat g\rangle_{\widehat G}$, of which the finite cyclic case is the instance proved here

items.strategy: Expand $\langle\mathcal F_Nf,\mathcal F_Ng\rangle=\sum_k(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)\overline{(\mathcal F_Ng)(k)}$ using the definition, conjugate the second factor and interchange the finite sums by the finite Fubini rule of [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], with the scalar factors moved through the sums by distributivity ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) and the conjugation laws ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). The inner sum is $\sum_ke^{-2\pi ik(x-y)/N}=N\delta_{x=y}$ by [[lem-orthogonality-of-characters-on-a-finite-cyclic-group]], and the prefactor $N^{-1/2}\cdot N^{-1/2}=N^{-1}$ cancels the $N$ ([[lem-rational-power-laws]]). The norm identity is the case $g=f$ with $z\overline z=|z|^2$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). The identity is exactly the statement that $\mathcal F_N$ is an isometry for the counting inner product; invertibility of $\mathcal F_N$ is not asserted here.

items.title: The DFT turns cyclic convolution into a scaled pointwise product
items.statement: Let $N\ge1$ and $f,g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then for every $k\in\mathbb Z$ $$(\mathcal F_N(f*g))(k)=\sqrt N\,(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)(\mathcal F_Ng)(k),$$ where $*$ is the unnormalised cyclic convolution of [[def-cyclic-convolution-on-z-mod-n]] and $\sqrt N=N^{1/2}$. Equivalently, the unnormalised transform $X$ of [[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]] satisfies $X_k(f*g)=X_k(f)X_k(g)$ for every $k$: with the engineering normalisation the convolution law has no extra factor.

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Fourier Analysis, Distributions, and Constant-Coefficient Linear PDE (author PDF)
references.locator: §11, formulas (11.30)-(11.31): the transform of a discrete convolution is the product of the transforms

references.title: MIT 18.310 lecture 23, The Finite Fourier Transform and the Fast Fourier Transform Algorithm (course page)
references.locator: headings 3-4: the transform converts polynomial products (hence convolution) into pointwise products

items.strategy: Substitute both definitions and interchange the finite sums: $$(\mathcal F_N(f*g))(k)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z/N}f(y)e^{-2\pi iky/N}\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z/N}g(z)e^{-2\pi ikz/N},$$ where, for fixed $y$, the substitution $z=x-y$ reindexes the sum over $x$ ([[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]]). The two inner sums are $N^{1/2}(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)$ and $N^{1/2}(\mathcal F_Ng)(k)$, so the prefactor gives $\sqrt N$ ([[lem-rational-power-laws]]). The unnormalised form follows from $X_k=\sqrt N\,\mathcal F_N$ ([[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]]). The lemma distinguishes cyclic from linear convolution ([[cex-linear-and-cyclic-convolution-are-not-the-same-without-zero-padding]]).

items.title: $\mathcal F_N^2$ is reflection and $\mathcal F_N^4$ is the identity
items.statement: Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Define the reflection $Rf$ by $(Rf)(x):=f(-x)$. Then $\mathcal F_N^2f=Rf$ and $\mathcal F_N^4=\mathrm{id}$; consequently $\mathcal F_N^2$ is an involution and $\mathcal F_N^3=\mathcal F_N^{-1}$. At $N=1$ and $N=2$ the reflection is the identity, so $\mathcal F_N^2=\mathrm{id}$ there.

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Fourier Analysis, Distributions, and Constant-Coefficient Linear PDE (author PDF)
references.locator: §11, formulas (11.1)-(11.6) and Proposition 11.2: the transform pair and the exponent bookkeeping behind the fourth-power identity

references.title: MIT 18.310 lecture 23, The Finite Fourier Transform and the Fast Fourier Transform Algorithm (course page)
references.locator: heading 3: the forward and inverse transforms differ by the sign of the root, so two applications recover the reflection of the input

items.strategy: Expand $$\mathcal F_N^2f(x)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\Big(N^{-1/2}\sum_{y=0}^{N-1}f(y)e^{-2\pi iky/N}\Big)e^{-2\pi ikx/N},$$ interchange the finite sums and evaluate the inner $k$-sum by [[lem-orthogonality-of-characters-on-a-finite-cyclic-group]] as $N\delta_{x=-y}$; the prefactor cancels and the surviving term is $f(-x)$. Applying the identity twice gives $\mathcal F_N^4f(x)=\mathcal F_N^2(\mathcal F_N^2f)(x)=(\mathcal F_N^2f)(-x)=f(-(-x))=f(x)$, using $-(-x)=x$ in $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-integers-modulo-n-basic-algebra]]). In particular $R^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $\mathcal F_N^2$ is an involution; combine with [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]] to read $\mathcal F_N^3=\mathcal F_N^{-1}$.

items.title: The unnormalised engineering DFT and its conversion to the unitary transform
items.statement: Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. The **unnormalised (engineering) discrete Fourier transform** of $f$ is the $N$-periodic function $X(f):\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ defined by $$X_k(f):=\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,e^{-2\pi ikx/N}=\sqrt N\,(\mathcal F_Nf)(k),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.$$ The two transforms determine each other by the conversions $X_k(f)=\sqrt N(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)$ and $(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}X_k(f)$. The inverse formulas are $f(x)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)e^{2\pi ikx/N}$ and, in the engineering normalisation, $$f(x)=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X_k(f)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},\qquad x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z.$$ This is the convention in which the radix-two algorithm of [[def-recursive-radix-two-fast-fourier-transform]] computes its output; the unitary normalisation is recovered by the explicit rescaling $2^{-m/2}$ at length $N=2^m$.

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Fourier Analysis, Distributions, and Constant-Coefficient Linear PDE (author PDF)
references.locator: §12, formula (12.1) and the surrounding computation counts: the transform computed numerically before normalisation

references.title: MIT 18.310 lecture 23, The Finite Fourier Transform and the Fast Fourier Transform Algorithm (course page)
references.locator: heading 3: forward evaluations $p(z^k)$ and the inverse $a_s=(1/n)\sum_kp_kz^{-sk}$ with the factor $1/n$ visible

items.strategy: Definitional conversion: $X_k(f)=\sqrt N\,\mathcal F_Nf(k)$ is immediate from [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]] and [[lem-rational-power-laws]]; the $N$-periodicity of $X(f)$ is that of $\mathcal F_Nf$. The inverse formulas are [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]] multiplied by $N^{-1/2}\cdot N^{1/2}=1$ and rewritten with $X$. State the ratio $X/\mathcal F_N=\sqrt N$ and its inverse $1/\sqrt N=N^{-1/2}$ once, so that no later item mixes the two normalisations: the cyclic-convolution law [[lem-finite-fourier-transform-converts-cyclic-convolution-to-scaled-product]] and the FFT correctness/complexity theorems [[thm-radix-two-fft-correctness]], [[thm-radix-two-fft-arithmetic-complexity]] are both stated for $X$, and the unitary transform is recovered by the single rescaling stated above.

items.title: The radix-two even/odd factorisation of the DFT
items.statement: Let $M\ge1$, $N=2M$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Define the even and odd parts $e,o\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/M}$ by $e(r):=f(2r)$ and $o(r):=f(2r+1)$ for $r\in\mathbb Z/M\mathbb Z$, where $2r$ and $2r+1$ denote the classes in $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ of the corresponding integers (the maps $r\mapsto2r$ and $r\mapsto2r+1$ from $\mathbb Z/M\mathbb Z$ to $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ are well-defined and injective with disjoint images, which together exhaust $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$). Let $X(f)$, $X(e)$, $X(o)$ be the unnormalised transforms of [[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]], the latter two extended $M$-periodically to $\mathbb Z$. Then for every $k\in\mathbb Z$ $$X_k(f)=X_k(e)+e^{-2\pi ik/N}X_k(o),\qquad X_{k+M}(f)=X_k(e)-e^{-2\pi ik/N}X_k(o).$$ Thus an $N$-point transform is computed from the two $M$-point transforms of its even and odd parts and the twiddle factors $e^{-2\pi ik/N}$; this is the radix-two (decimation-in-time) step of the fast Fourier transform.

references.title: MIT 18.310 lecture 23, The Finite Fourier Transform and the Fast Fourier Transform Algorithm (course page)
references.locator: heading 4: the reduction of an n-point transform to the two s-point transforms of the even and odd coefficient sequences, with the $z^j$ twiddle in the odd evaluations

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Fourier Analysis, Distributions, and Constant-Coefficient Linear PDE (author PDF)
references.locator: §12, (12.8)-(12.11) and Proposition 12.1: the mirror-image decimation-in-frequency form, which the proof absorbs as the equivalent formulation

items.strategy: Partition the defining sum over $\mathbb Z/N=2\mathbb Z/M\sqcup(2\mathbb Z/M+1)$ and reindex each part by $r\in\mathbb Z/M$; well-definedness of $r\mapsto2r$ and $r\mapsto2r+1$ uses $2(r+M)=2r+N$ and $(2r+1)+N$ ([[thm-integers-modulo-n-basic-algebra]], [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]]). The character identity is $\chi_{-k}(2r)=e^{-2\pi ikr/M}$ and $\chi_{-k}(2r+1)=e^{-2\pi ik/N}\chi_{-k}(2r)$, which is the addition law for the exponential plus the character computation of [[ex-pontryagin-dual-of-a-finite-cyclic-group]]. For the second identity use $M$-periodicity of $k\mapsto X_k(e),X_k(o)$ and $e^{-2\pi i(k+M)/N}=e^{-2\pi ik/N}e^{-\pi i}=-e^{-2\pi ik/N}$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]). Taylor's Proposition 12.1 proves the decimation-in-frequency variant (input halves, output parities); record that it is the mirror of the displayed identity rather than a second independent result.

items.title: The recursive radix-two fast Fourier transform
items.statement: Let $m\in\mathbb N$ and $N=2^m$. Define the **radix-two fast Fourier transform** $\operatorname{FFT}_m:\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}\to\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ by recursion on $m$: $\operatorname{FFT}_0=\mathrm{id}$, and for $m\ge1$, given $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^m}$ with even and odd parts $e,o\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^{m-1}}$ and $E=\operatorname{FFT}_{m-1}(e)$, $O=\operatorname{FFT}_{m-1}(o)$ extended $2^{m-1}$-periodically to $\mathbb Z$, set $$\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k):=E(k)+e^{-2\pi ik/2^m}O(k),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.$$ Then $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k+2^m)=\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k)$ for every $k$, so $\operatorname{FFT}_m$ is a well-defined map on $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^m}$; the recursion terminates after $m$ levels at the base case $N=1$, where it returns the input, and at each level it forms the even and odd parts and one combine per subproblem. The algorithm computes the unnormalised transform $X$ of [[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]] ([[thm-radix-two-fft-correctness]]); the unitary transform is recovered by the rescaling $2^{-m/2}$.

references.title: MIT 18.310 lecture 23, The Finite Fourier Transform and the Fast Fourier Transform Algorithm (course page)
references.locator: heading 4: iterate the even/odd reduction until degree 0, evaluating the two $s$-point transforms in parallel

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Fourier Analysis, Distributions, and Constant-Coefficient Linear PDE (author PDF)
references.locator: §12, (12.8)-(12.23): the inductive procedure and its iterative implementation, with the base case $G_0=\{1\}$

items.strategy: Apply ordinary recursion to the tagged state set A={(m,g):g:F_m→F_m}, where F_m=C^{Z/2^m}; start at (0,id_F0). For each tagged state (m,g), the even/odd split and the combine formula define a total map F_{m+1}→F_{m+1}; prove it is well defined because the recursive outputs are 2^m-periodic and the twiddle is 2^{m+1}-periodic. The total step maps (m,g) to (m+1,g+). Recursion and induction recover the stated family FFT_m. Termination is immediate, and rescaling uses 2^{-m/2}=(2^m)^{-1/2}.

items.title: Correctness of the recursive radix-two FFT
items.statement: Let $m\in\mathbb N$, $N=2^m$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then $$\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k)=X_k(f)\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z,$$ where $X(f)$ is the unnormalised $N$-point discrete Fourier transform of [[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]]. Equivalently $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)=2^{m/2}\,\mathcal F_Nf$; consequently the algorithm returns the unitary transform after the single rescaling $2^{-m/2}$, and it does so for every input of length $2^m$.

references.locator: heading 4: the even/odd reduction is exact at every level, so iterating it returns the evaluations

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Fourier Analysis, Distributions, and Constant-Coefficient Linear PDE (author PDF)
references.locator: §12, Proposition 12.1 with (12.11)-(12.23): the inductive identities, for the mirror decimation-in-frequency form

items.strategy: Induction on m. Base m=0: the length-one transform is the identity. For the successor, fix m≥0 and assume P(m); set N=2^{m+1} and M=2^m, and split an input in F_{m+1} into even/odd parts in F_m. By the recursive definition, FFT_{m+1}(f)(k)=FFT_m(e)(k)+e^{-2πik/2^{m+1}}FFT_m(o)(k). The induction hypothesis gives X_k(e), X_k(o), and the radix-two factorisation with N=2M gives X_k(f), proving P(m+1). Then rescale by 2^{-m/2} to recover the unitary transform; correctness does not assert a speed or stability bound.

items.title: The radix-two FFT uses $O(N\log_2N)$ complex arithmetic operations
items.statement: Let $T_m$ be the number of complex-number multiplications and additions performed by the recursion of [[def-recursive-radix-two-fast-fourier-transform]] on an input of length $N=2^m$, counted as the operations of the two recursive subproblems of length $2^{m-1}$ plus, at the top level, the $2^m$ twiddle multiplications $e^{-2\pi ik/2^m}O(k)$ and the $2^m$ additions $E(k)+\cdot$ needed to form all $2^m$ values, and with no other operations counted. Then $T_0=0$, $T_m\le2T_{m-1}+2\cdot2^m$ for $m\ge1$, and $$T_m\le2m\,2^m=2N\log_2N.$$ In particular $T_m=O(m2^m)$, so the algorithm uses $O(N\log_2N)$ complex arithmetic operations on inputs of length $N=2^m$, whereas independent direct evaluation of all $N$ coefficients uses $n(n-1)$ additions and $n^2$ multiplications (Taylor §12). The count is of arithmetic operations only: integer index arithmetic, twiddle evaluation, memory access and bit complexity are not counted, and no numerical-stability claim is made.

references.locator: heading 4: at each reduction $s$ additions, $s$ subtractions and $s$ multiplications reduce the problem by a factor of two

items.strategy: Unroll the recurrence: dividing $U_m:=T_m/2^m$ by the level size turns $T_m\le2T_{m-1}+2\cdot2^m$ into $U_m\le U_{m-1}+2$, so $U_m\le2m$ and $T_m\le2m2^m$ by induction ([[thm-induction-principle]], [[lem-power-laws]]). Use the item's local eventual-domination definition of $O$ to infer $T_m=O(m2^m)$ from the explicit constant $2$, then rewrite $m=\log_2(2^m)$ via [[def-logarithm-to-a-base]]. The operation model is the theorem's explicit hypothesis and must be restated in the item: only complex multiplications and additions inside the recursion and combine, no twiddle evaluation or memory traffic; this matches Taylor's counting to within constants (kn additions and kn/2 multiplications against our $2m2^m$ upper bound).

items.title: Mixed-radix factorisation for composite lengths (recorded, not proved here)
items.statement: **Recorded, not proved here.** The radix-two step is the case $R=2$ of a mixed-radix (Cooley-Tukey) factorisation: for $N=RS$ the input indices split into the $R$ residue classes modulo $R$, the $N$-point transform reduces to $R$ transforms of length $S$ combined with twiddle factors, and Taylor §12 Exercise 4 records the generalisation to $n=3^k$ and to products of small primes. For prime $N$ no such nontrivial factorisation exists, and the bound of [[thm-radix-two-fft-arithmetic-complexity]] is proved only for $N$ a power of two: it is not a claim about prime lengths, and no $O(N\log N)$ bound for arbitrary $N$ is asserted on this page.

external_dependency.exact_statement: Taylor, §12, Exercise 4: "Generalize the FFT algorithm to a cyclic group $\Gamma_n$ with $n=3^k$. Also, generalize to the case $n=p_1\cdots p_k$ where $p_j$ are 'small' primes." The main text of §12 restricts the displayed recursion to the case $n=2^k$.
external_dependency.local_proof_attempt: Not reconstructed here: the design assigns this row proof provenance not-supplied. The general step would replace the two-class partition by the $R$ residue classes modulo $R$ and use twiddle factors $e^{-2\pi i\cdot/N}$ on the resulting short transforms, but no local proof is written on this page and the remark is a leaf.
external_dependency.necessity: Prevents the $O(N\log_2N)$ theorem for powers of two from being read as a statement about every $N$, and records where composite-length mixed-radix recursions come from without claiming them locally.

title: Finite Fourier Analysis and the Fast Fourier Transform — Examples

items.title: The unitary DFT for $N=1$ and $N=2$
items.statement: For $N=1$ the unitary transform of [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]] is the identity, $\mathcal F_1f=f$, with matrix $[1]$. For $N=2$, writing $f=(f_0,f_1)$, $$\mathcal F_2(f_0,f_1)=2^{-1/2}(f_0+f_1,\ f_0-f_1),$$ whose matrix $\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ is real symmetric, unitary and equal to its own inverse. Since the reflection $x\mapsto-x$ is the identity on $\mathbb Z/1$ and on $\mathbb Z/2$, the fourth-power identity of [[lem-dft-squares-to-reflection-and-has-fourth-power-identity]] reads $\mathcal F_N^2=\mathcal F_N^4=\mathrm{id}$ for $N=1,2$, consistent with [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]].

items.strategy: Verification by direct evaluation: at $N=1$ the only term is $f([0])$ with coefficient $1^{-1/2}=1$; at $N=2$ one has $e^{-\pi ik}=(-1)^k$, giving the displayed pair, and the matrix identity $A^2=I$ is checked by multiplying $1/\sqrt2\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ by itself. The reflection clause uses $-x=x$ in $\mathbb Z/1$ and $\mathbb Z/2$ ([[thm-integers-modulo-n-basic-algebra]]).

items.title: Cyclic convolution on $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$ via the DFT
items.statement: On $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$ let $f=(1,1,0,0)$ and $g=(1,1,0,0)$. Their unnormalised transforms are $X(f)=X(g)=(2,1-i,0,1+i)$, so the engineering form of [[lem-finite-fourier-transform-converts-cyclic-convolution-to-scaled-product]] gives $X(f*g)=(4,-2i,0,2i)$; inverse transforming, $(f*g)(x)=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^3X_k(f*g)e^{2\pi ikx/4}$ gives $(f*g)=(1,2,1,0)$. Direct evaluation of $(f*g)(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z/4}f(y)g(x-y)$ gives the same tuple: $1,2,1,0$. In this instance the length is large enough that no wrap-around occurs, so the cyclic convolution equals the linear convolution $(1,2,1,0)$ of the coefficient sequences.

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Fourier Analysis, Distributions, and Constant-Coefficient Linear PDE (author PDF)
references.locator: §11, (11.30)-(11.31): the discrete convolution and its transform law, here computed for a four-point example

items.strategy: Direct computation of both sides: $X_k(f)=1+e^{-2\pi ik/4}=1+(-i)^k$ gives $(2,1-i,0,1+i)$; squaring componentwise gives $(4,-2i,0,2i)$; the inverse engineering formula has the prefactor $1/4$ and the values $e^{2\pi ikx/4}\in\{1,i,-1,-i\}$ produce $(1,2,1,0)$. The direct sum over $y$ is evaluated at all four classes. Compare with [[cex-linear-and-cyclic-convolution-are-not-the-same-without-zero-padding]] for the length regime in which the two notions differ.

items.title: The four-point radix-two FFT executed in full
items.statement: For $N=4=2^2$ and $f=(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)$, the recursion of [[def-recursive-radix-two-fast-fourier-transform]] takes the even part $e=(f_0,f_2)$ and the odd part $o=(f_1,f_3)$. The two length-two unnormalised transforms are $E=(f_0+f_2,\ f_0-f_2)$ and $O=(f_1+f_3,\ f_1-f_3)$, extended $2$-periodically, and the combine with twiddle $e^{-2\pi ik/4}=(-i)^k$ gives $$X_0=f_0+f_1+f_2+f_3,\quad X_2=f_0-f_1+f_2-f_3,$$ $$X_1=f_0-if_1-f_2+if_3,\quad X_3=f_0+if_1-f_2-if_3.$$ These agree with direct evaluation of $X_k=\sum_{x=0}^3f_xe^{-2\pi ikx/4}$, as [[thm-radix-two-fft-correctness]] requires, and the merge uses $O(4\log_24)$ complex operations ([[thm-radix-two-fft-arithmetic-complexity]]).

items.strategy: Execute both levels by hand: $E(0)=f_0+f_2$, $E(1)=f_0-f_2$, $O(0)=f_1+f_3$, $O(1)=f_1-f_3$; then $X_k=E(k)+(-i)^kO(k)$ for $k=0,1$ and, using the second branch of [[lem-radix-two-even-odd-dft-factorisation]], $X_{k+2}=E(k)-(-i)^kO(k)$; substituting $E,O$ gives the displayed four values. Compare each with the direct sum. The check exercises the base case $m=0$ implicitly through the two-point transforms.

items.title: Cyclic convolution wraps a high coefficient without zero padding
items.statement: For $f=g=(1,1)$ on $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ the cyclic convolution of [[def-cyclic-convolution-on-z-mod-n]] is $(f*g)(0)=1\cdot1+1\cdot1=2$ and $(f*g)(1)=1\cdot1+1\cdot1=2$, so $f*g=(2,2)$. The product $(1+z)(1+z)=1+2z+z^2$ of the associated polynomials has coefficient sequence $(1,2,1)$, and reducing exponents modulo $2$ (that is, modulo $z^2-1$) sends $(1,2,1)$ to $(1+1,2)=(2,2)$. The coefficient $1$ of $z^2$ has wrapped into degree $0$. Zero-padding both inputs to length $N'\ge3$ gives the cyclic convolution $(1,2,1,0,\dots)$, which equals the linear convolution; without sufficient padding the two notions differ, and the product law [[lem-finite-fourier-transform-converts-cyclic-convolution-to-scaled-product]] computes the cyclic, not the linear, convolution.

items.strategy: Direct computation of the cyclic sum at each of the two classes, side by side with the coefficient product $1+2z+z^2$; the reduction $z^2\mapsto1$ (equivalently $x\cdot x^1$ reindexed modulo $2$ in the convolution sum) exhibits the wrap. Verify the padded case by the same sum with the inputs $(1,1,0,0)$: the length-four cyclic convolution is $(1,2,1,0)$, matching the linear coefficient list. No claim is made that cyclic convolutions are unusable; the point is that the padding length must be at least the number of coefficients of the linear product.

items.title: The radix-two split fails for odd $N$
items.statement: The radix-two step of [[lem-radix-two-even-odd-dft-factorisation]] and the recursion of [[def-recursive-radix-two-fast-fourier-transform]] require an even length. For $N=3$ the doubling map $r\mapsto2r$ is a bijection of $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$ (its inverse is doubling again, since $2\cdot2=4\equiv1$), so $2\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$; likewise $r\mapsto2r+1$ is a bijection. Hence the 'even' and 'odd' classes each exhaust $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$ and do not partition it into two subproblems of size $M=N/2$; moreover $M=3/2$ is not an integer, so the twiddle identity $e^{-2\pi iM/N}=-1$ used by the combine has no integer-length interpretation. This says nothing against direct evaluation of the three-point transform.

items.strategy: Direct computation in $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$: $2\cdot0=0$, $2\cdot1=2$, $2\cdot2=4\equiv1$, so doubling is the permutation $(0)(1\,2)$; adding $1$ gives the translated permutation. Hence each of the two attempted index sets is all of $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$, and no two-coset decomposition with $M=3/2$ exists. The counterexample tests only the algorithm's length hypothesis; it deliberately makes no hardness claim about odd-length transforms.
